title: Mantra repetition
hook: repeating a sacred name or mantra, often on beads

segments.voice: Yesterday, stilling the mind: Patanjali's definition of yoga, the mind's movements growing still. Your line was stilling. Did you catch a mood and name it, worry, memory, plan, before it shaped you? Day one thousand three hundred ninety-five.

A string of wooden beads hangs on a hook by a kitchen door, one spot worn smooth. Early, before the kettle, a hand takes it down. A thumb pulls one bead toward the palm. Lips move. A name is said, barely above a breath. Next bead. Same name. Next bead. Same name. No new words are added. Nothing is asked for. The kettle boils and is ignored for a moment longer. Yesterday the mind was a lake, moving in the wind. Today, a way of giving it one place to move. Today's word is japa.
screen: `BEADS BY THE KITCHEN DOOR.` → `ONE BEAD, ONE NAME.` → `NOTHING ADDED, NOTHING ASKED.`

segments.voice: Japa is the repetition of a sacred name or a mantra, said aloud, whispered, or held silently in the mind. Different Hindu communities repeat different names. Devotees of Shiva may repeat Om namah Shivaya. Devotees of Rama may repeat the name Ram. It is often counted on a string of beads called a mala, so the hand keeps the count and the mind doesn't have to. And it turns up in the very book we opened yesterday. In the Yoga Sutras, sutra one point twenty-seven says the word that expresses the Lord is the pranava, the sacred syllable Om. And the next sutra gives the practice in two parts: its repetition, japa, and dwelling on its meaning. Both halves, together. The book doesn't ask for sound alone, and it doesn't ask for meaning alone. It asks for the word, said again and again, with attention on what it points to. From that, the following sutra says, comes turning inward, and the clearing of what stands in the way. The Bhagavad Gita goes further. There, Krishna names, kind by kind, what he is among things, and among the forms of sacrifice, he says, he is japa, the sacrifice of repetition. A sacrifice that needs no fire, no food, no money. Only breath and a name. So japa isn't saying a word until it means nothing. In this picture it works the other way: the word is said so often that the mind, which moves all day, gets worn into one groove, like the smooth spot on the bead.
screen: `A SACRED NAME, AGAIN AND AGAIN.` · `BEADS KEEP THE COUNT.` · `REPETITION, AND ITS MEANING.` · `THE SACRIFICE OF REPETITION.` · then, large: `ONE GROOVE, LIKE THE SMOOTH BEAD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: repeat one word twenty-seven times. Choose the word first, and keep it. If you pray, a name from your own tradition. If you don't, a plain word like peace, or here. Count on your fingers: three rounds of nine is easy to keep. Say it softly, or just inside. On each one, let a little of the meaning come with it. When you lose count, don't start over in frustration. Just go on from where you think you were. The bell holds the time.
Japa. The repetition of a sacred name or mantra, often counted on beads, aloud, whispered or silent, with attention on its meaning. Today's word.
Your line: japa. Today, keep your word in your pocket. In a line, at a red light, on the stairs, say it once, slowly, and let it bring you back. Day one thousand three hundred ninety-five.

howItsDone: Hindus who practice japa repeat a mantra or a name of God such as Ram or Om namah Shivaya, often counting on a mala of beads, aloud, in a whisper, or silently.

fork.setup: you're repeating Om on your beads, and realize you've said it twenty times while planning lunch. by sutra 1.28, what's missing?
options: the meaning: attention on what the word points to.
fork.reveal: the sutra asks for two things together: the repetition, and dwelling on its meaning. you kept the sound and dropped the meaning. so you just pick it back up.

trapdoor: what you thought: japa is chanting something over and over until it means nothing.
what it means: repeating a sacred name or mantra, often on beads, so a moving mind gets one place to rest.
what a scholar hears: Yoga Sutras 1.27–28 name Om as the word for the Lord and pair its japa with dwelling on its meaning; in Gita 10.25 Krishna names japa among the sacrifices.

notes: Yoga Sutras 1.27 (tasya vachakah pranavah), 1.28 (taj-japas tad-artha-bhavanam) and 1.29 (pratyak-chetana and the removal of obstacles) paraphrased. Confirm.
Gita 10.25 ('of sacrifices I am the sacrifice of japa') paraphrased; Arnold 1885 wording not checked. 'One of each kind' summarizes the vibhuti list of chapter 10; confirm.
Examples of names (Om namah Shivaya for Shaiva devotees, Ram for devotees of Rama) are general; confirm they are fair.
